Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Velez (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Hemisphere Head of Product), Dan Wu (CTO), Alicia Park (ML Eng)

---
Summary (auto): quick hosted API walkthrough, demoed chat + text generation, showed streaming and retry behavior, discussed hosted vs dedicated and security concerns.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lena from Redwood, and with me is Marcus, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya: Good thanks, excited to see this. We're trying to understand latency and cost for the in-store assistant use case.
[00:12] Dan: Yep, and security, we have strict PII rules so wanna see what the hosted API implies for data retention.
[00:18] Marcus: Great, we'll jump in. Quick agenda: show the Hosted API for chat/text generation, streaming demo, key parameters like temperature/top-p/max_tokens, and cover retry semantics and rate limiting.
[00:30] Marcus: Alright I'm sharing my screen. So this is a sample request to /v1/chat/completions, same interface you'd use for streaming clients. You'll see I'm using the node SDK but curl works the same.
[00:42] Marcus: The body includes messages, model selection — we're using a small latency-optimized model for demo — and then the streaming flag. When you set stream:true you'll get token-level chunks.
[00:58] Priya: How smooth is the streaming? Our UI expects incremental sentence-level rendering.
[01:04] Marcus: In our tests it's pretty smooth — you can get tokens every 40-200ms depending on model and sequence length, but for production we recommend enabling our prefix cache and smaller batch windows to reduce latency jitter.
[01:20] Alicia: When you say prefix cache, is that the KV cache? I've seen it called KV cache elsewhere, sometimes transcribed as K V cash in notes.
[01:28] Marcus: Yes KV cache, key-value cache for transformer kv states. It helps especially for chat with long histories because we avoid recomputing prefix tokens.
[01:36] Dan: For the hosted plan, where is data stored? We have to ensure no long-term retention for PII.
[01:42] Lena: Good question. Hosted API defaults to short-term retention for telemetry and debugging, but we have configurable data retention and a zero-retention option on enterprise tiers. We also support customer-managed encryption keys (KMS/HSM) for Private and Dedicated. I'll follow up with our security pack.
[01:55] Priya: Do you have SOC 2 and ISO stuff?
[01:58] Lena: Yes SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001. We'll send the certs and audit guide after the call.
[02:04] Marcus: Back to the demo — here's an example of temperature and top_p. Higher temperature increases randomness, top_p controls nucleus sampling. For deterministic outputs set temperature 0 and top_p 1.
[02:16] Marcus: Also max_tokens and stop sequences — we recommend setting a sensible max to control cost. For assistant-style chat set about 150-300 tokens for short replies.
[02:28] Priya: What's your recommendation for retry logic? We have intermittent 503s on our current provider and want to avoid duplicate side effects.
[02:36] Marcus: For idempotent requests like text generation we recommend an exponential backoff with jitter and a request idempotency key on your side. Redwood's client libraries expose a retry helper. Also, for function calls or when you trigger downstream actions, we advise implementing a dedupe token or server-side idempotency key so retries don't cause duplicate writes.
[02:56] Dan: Do you have automatic retry on the SDK?
[02:59] Marcus: Yes the SDK has a default retry policy for 5xx/429, configurable. For stricter control you can turn it off and implement custom logic.
[03:06] Alicia: Any rate limit guidance? Our traffic pattern has spiky bursts during peak hours.
[03:12] Marcus: Hosted tier has rate limits by default, and you can request quota increases. For predictable spikes we recommend Dedicated — you get reserved GPU capacity and predictable throughput. For Hosted, we also have burst capacity options and smart routing to other regions/models as a fallback.
[03:28] Priya: How does the fallback work? If your primary model is busy, will it route to a slightly cheaper or smaller model? We're concerned about quality changes.
[03:36] Lena: Yes we can configure fallback policies — route by latency or cost. We also provide model variants with verified performance profiles so you can choose a compatible fallback that minimizes quality regression. We log score deltas in the Console so you can detect regressions.
[03:50] Marcus: I'm going to demo streaming now. I'm sending a prompt that asks for a store assistant reply.
[04:00] [Screen shows incremental tokens arriving]
[04:10] Marcus: You can see tokens arriving in the client. There's an event for 'delta' and finalization. If you lose the connection the server keeps the output for a short window so you can resume — this is controlled by the response window setting.
[04:26] Priya: What's that window length?
[04:29] Marcus: Default is 60 seconds for hosted; can be extended for enterprise.
[04:34] Dan: For benchmarking, what metrics should we collect? Latency at p50/p95/p99, tokens-per-second, cost per 1k tokens?
[04:42] Marcus: Exactly. Also measure cold-start latency (first request to a cold model), steady-state throughput, and tails. We'll include a benchmark spreadsheet template.
[04:52] Priya: On integration, how do we handle auth — SSO for our internal dashboards?
[04:58] Lena: For the Console we support SAML SSO and SSO provisioning. For API keys we have scoped keys with route-level permissions and expiration.
[05:06] Alicia: For encryption at rest, are keys managed by Redwood or can we supply our own?
[05:11] Lena: Both — hosted uses Redwood-managed keys by default; on Dedicated/Private you can use your KMS or HSM.
[05:18] Marcus: Quick demo of parameters: I'll show temperature 0.2 versus 0.9 so you can see output diversity.
[05:24] [Demo shows two outputs; the 0.2 one is concise, the 0.9 one is more creative and longer]
[05:36] Priya: For the assistant persona, can we bias responses or inject system prompts?
[05:40] Marcus: Yes you can include system messages, or use instruction templates. We also support fine-grained prompt templates and response constraints. For hard constraints we recommend function calling or structured output with validation.
[05:52] Dan: Any built-in tools for cost optimization? We have thousands of daily queries, mostly short answers.
[05:58] Marcus: Redwood Optimize suggests batching configs, model/quantization recommendations and caching rules. For short queries, batching may not help latency, but prefix/KV caching and using smaller quantized models can reduce cost significantly. We'll show a cost breakdown in Console.
[06:14] Priya: About model versions, how do you manage rollouts? We need canary testing.
[06:19] Lena: Console supports rollouts: canaries, A/B tests, and automatic fallback if quality drops. You can pin versions and route a percentage of traffic.
[06:29] Alicia: For the pilot, what's a quick way to test with our data?
[06:32] Marcus: Best is to provide a prompt set and traffic profile; we'll run a small benchmark on Hosted with your prompt set and report latency and cost numbers. If results show high latency or cost, we'll propose Dedicated sizing and quantization options.
[06:45] Priya: Any legal/procure constraints? We'll need a DPA and security questionnaire.
[06:50] Lena: We'll attach the DPA and standard security questionnaire. For enterprise deals we do standard SLAs and can support additional compliance clauses.
[06:58] Marcus: Closing the demo — quick recap of streaming behavior, param guidance, retries/backoff, and security options.
[07:06] Priya: Sounds good. A couple of quick, smaller questions: what about tokenization differences — we run non-English product names which sometimes split oddly.
[07:15] Marcus: Good point — tokenizer differences can change token counts; we provide tokenization tools and recommend measuring tokens on sample prompts to estimate cost. We also support custom pre-processing to handle product names as single tokens via special tokens in some models.
[07:30] Dan: Is there a sandbox/test environment?
[07:33] Lena: Yes we can provision a trial account with free credits and a test API key. We'll include rate limits for the sandbox.
[07:39] Priya: For the benchmark, can Redwood run the tests or do we need to run them?
[07:43] Marcus: We can run the initial benchmark if you give us the prompt set and allow a short-lived test key. We'll share the results and the spreadsheet with p50/p95/p99 and cost estimates.
[07:53] Alicia: One more on retries: if a streaming response partially arrives and client reconnects, is the chunk replayed or do we restart?
[07:59] Marcus: You can resume if you keep a request id and the server holds a short window of the response. Otherwise clients implement replay from last confirmed token. That's why client-side idempotency is important.
[08:12] Priya: Ok great. Let's summarize next steps.
[08:15] Lena: Lena to send pricing + security pack and SOC2/ISO artifacts; Marcus to set up benchmark harness and share sample request templates; Priya/Alicia to share prompt set and traffic profile. We'll aim to have the benchmark run next week.
[08:28] Dan: Timeline wise, if the benchmark looks good, we may move to a short pilot on Hosted with an eye toward Dedicated for peak traffic by Q2.
[08:36] Lena: Perfect, we'll follow up via email and attach the DPA and trial instructions.
[08:42] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[08:44] Lena: Thanks, talk soon.
[08:46] [Call ends]

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker label errors and minor word swaps (e.g., K V cash -> KV cache). Some timestamps approximate.
